title: Sell Mineral Rights in Westminster, CO
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Westminster, CO | Adams County
metaDescription: Westminster restricted new oil and gas drilling within city limits in 2021. See what that means for a legacy mineral interest under the city.
heroLead: Westminster's city council moved to restrict new oil and gas development within city limits, which fundamentally changes how a mineral interest here should be valued.
intro: Westminster is one of the few Front Range cities to take direct legislative action against new oil and gas drilling, adopting restrictions on new development within city limits in 2021 following years of resident concern over proposed sites near neighborhoods. For mineral owners, that decision doesn't erase the value of an interest under the city, but it does mean pricing has to account for local policy as much as geology.

We still work with Westminster owners regularly, because a restriction on new surface locations inside the city doesn't touch what's happening on the ground just outside it, where operators continue to permit and drill within the surrounding Adams and Weld County acreage.

sections.heading: What Westminster's restrictions actually mean
paragraphs: The city's action targeted new surface locations and development within its limits, using the local siting authority granted to municipalities under SB 19-181. It doesn't retroactively void existing leases or mineral ownership, and it doesn't necessarily block a horizontal well bottomed under the city from a pad located outside Westminster's boundaries, but it does substantially reduce the odds of a new surface location appearing inside city limits in the near term.

sections.heading: Legacy interests from the pre-development era
paragraphs: As with most of Adams County, land under Westminster's neighborhoods was agricultural long before it was residential, and mineral interests severed from that farmland are common. Many current owners are heirs with limited direct knowledge of what their family originally reserved, which is why the first step is always confirming the chain of title.

sections.heading: Pricing given the local policy landscape
paragraphs: We factor Westminster's restrictions directly into our valuation, weighing the reduced likelihood of near-term surface development against the possibility of eventual inclusion in an outside horizontal unit, and price accordingly rather than assuming either extreme. We also pull the Adams County Clerk and Recorder chain of title to confirm your fractional share before putting a number in front of you.

faqs.question: Did Westminster's restrictions eliminate my mineral rights?
faqs.answer: No, they restrict new surface development within city limits, but they don't void existing mineral ownership or leases. We factor the restriction into how we price the interest.

faqs.question: Could a well still be drilled under Westminster from outside the city?
faqs.answer: It's possible via a horizontal lateral from a pad outside city limits, depending on section geometry. We check current and plausible unit boundaries before valuing your interest.

faqs.question: Is my interest still worth selling given the restrictions?
faqs.answer: Yes, though it prices more conservatively than an interest in an area without local restrictions. We explain that reasoning clearly when we quote.

faqs.question: Do the restrictions apply to acreage just outside city limits?
faqs.answer: No, Westminster's action only covers land inside the city boundary. Adjacent Adams and Weld County acreage isn't affected by the city's local policy.
